sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Kǒngzǐ** (*kongzi*) — Confucius, Moral Teaching, Ritual · Master Kong — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Confucius, Moral Teaching, Ritual". The name means "Master Kong"[^1].

**Kǒngzǐ** belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is associated with confucius, moral teaching, ritual.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Kǒngzǐ** and serves its temple at [kongzi.com](https://punicodex.com/kongzi/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *kongzi* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^2].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Chinese characters as **孔子**. Etymologically it means "Master Kong"[^1].

Kǒng (孔) the clan name; zǐ (子) 'master' — the honorific title of the philosopher Confucius (Kong Qiu).

The ASCII form *kongzi* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Kǒngzǐ** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **k** → **K** — Same, capitalized
- **o** → **ǒ** — Caron tone mark
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **g** → **g** — Same
- **z** → **z** — Same
- **i** → **ǐ** — Caron tone mark

The canonical temple for this name is served at **kongzi.com**[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/kongzi/** — Chinese Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **K** — Initial character of the restored form Kǒngzǐ.
- **ǒngzǐ** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Chinese tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'KONGZI' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — Kǒngzǐ, the restored Unicode form of the name

Kǒngzǐ is Tier 1 because the Chinese form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

sections.body: The name is written in Chinese characters as **孔子**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *kongzi* and the PuniCodex restoration **Kǒngzǐ** are measured: the restoration preserves its pitch accent of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The stories of **Kǒngzǐ** circulate within the Chinese corpus, where the figure embodies confucius, moral teaching, ritual.[^1]

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Kǒngzǐ is attested in the canonical Chinese sources as a figure associated with confucius, moral teaching, ritual.[^1]

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Master Kong" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Kǒngzǐ**, or Confucius, is the Spring-and-Autumn period teacher whose sayings were compiled in the *Analects*. He advocated rén (humaneness), lǐ (ritual propriety), and xiào (filial piety) as the foundations of a harmonious society.[^1] Later dynasties elevated him to the status of culture-hero and patron of education, though he presented himself as a transmitter rather than an innovator. The *Analects* preserve his dialogues with disciples on governance, learning, and ritual, forming one of the most influential educational canons in world history.[^1]

sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Kǒngzǐ appears within the Chinese tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.[^1]

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[caishen|Cáishén]], [[change|Cháng'é]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], [[guandi|Guāndì]], and [[guanyin|Guānyīn]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Kǒngzǐ continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Chinese tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.[^1] Confucian teachings shaped state ideology, civil-service examination systems, and family ethics across East Asia for more than two millennia.[^1]

sections.label: Classical Texts
sections.body:
The **Analects (*Lúnyǔ*)** is the foundational record of Kǒngzǐ's conversations with disciples on ritual, virtue, and governance.[^1] The **Mencius** and **Xunzi** expand his teachings, while the **Zuǒzhuàn** and **Shǐjì** supply biographical and historical context.[^2]

Together these texts form the Wǔjīng and Sìshū canon that dominated East Asian education for two millennia.

sources.citation: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), biography of Confucius.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Daoist Sources
sections.body:
The **Zhuangzi** frequently invokes Kǒngzǐ as a foil for Daoist irony, placing him in dialogues with Laozi and recluses who expose the limits of ritual knowledge.[^1] Later **Dàozàng** hagiographies appropriated Confucius as a guardian of moral order, while Daoist ritual incorporated Confucian propriety into its liturgy.[^2]

The Confucian-Daoist tension became a defining structure of Chinese thought.

sources.citation: Daoist Canon (Daozang), ritual and hagiographic texts.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Buddhist Sources
sections.body:
Chinese Buddhism engaged deeply with Kǒngzǐ's ethics: apocryphal sutras such as the **Xiào jīng** and **Yúlánpén sūtra** harmonised filial piety with Buddhist salvation.[^1] The **Sānlùn** and **Tiāntái** schools used Confucian vocabulary to translate Indian categories.[^2]

Kǒngzǐ thus became part of a three-teachings (*sānjiào*) synthesis in which Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism shared moral authority.

sources.citation: Teiser, The Ghost Festival in Medieval China.

sections.label: Calligraphy & Script
sections.body:
The title **孔子** (Master Kong) is among the most copied phrases in Chinese calligraphy, executed in **seal, clerical, regular, running, and cursive scripts** across steles and hanging scrolls.[^1] Temple tablets at Qūfù present the name in formal **kǎishū**, while scholar-officials used it to demonstrate brush discipline.[^2]

The Unicode restoration **Kǒngzǐ** marks the third-tone contours that distinguish the honorific title from its flat ASCII form.

sections.body: Kǒngzǐ embodies confucius, moral teaching, ritual in the Chinese imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.[^1]
